A 52-year-old Bangladeshi man was referred to ENT for a 1-week history of odynophagia and a persistent sensation of a foreign body in his throat following fish-bone impaction. He had presented to the Emergency Department with similar symptoms and was diagnosed with a right tonsillar foreign body. He denied dysphagia, dyspnea, otalgia, or weight loss. His social history was notable for moderate tobacco use and habitual betel-nut chewing.

On examination, there was no visible fish bone. Instead, a protruding lesion was observed through the right palatine tonsil; it was hard, mobile, well-delineated, nontender, and yellowish-white in color. Flexible fibreoptic nasopharyngoscopy showed no mucosal ulceration or mass elsewhere in the upper aerodigestive tract, and no cervical lymphadenopathy was palpable. A lateral neck radiograph revealed no fish bone but demonstrated a uniform, ovoid calcification overlying the right tonsillar region abutting the mandibular ramus.

A 38-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of hypertension first noted at age 24 during pregnancy and again at age 38 after a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She had been diagnosed with splenomegaly of unknown cause at age 21; her younger brother had a similar finding. During her admission for hemorrhage, she underwent a decompressive craniectomy and was noted to have:  
- Normochromic microcytic anemia and thrombocytopenia on full blood examination; other laboratory tests, including thyroid function, cortisol, aldosterone–renin ratio, urinary metanephrines, and renal function, were unremarkable.  
- Lipid profile showed low HDL and elevated triglycerides.  
- Renal Doppler ultrasound excluded renal artery stenosis but revealed incidental bilateral adrenal lesions and hepatosplenomegaly.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed bilateral adrenal lesions (32 HU noncontrast; absolute washout 76.5%, relative washout 39%) that were unchanged after 8 months, and gross hepatosplenomegaly with dilated portal and splenic veins.  
She had no symptoms of adrenal hormone excess, and her blood pressure was controlled on a single antihypertensive agent.

A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

A 60-year-old man with hypertension and Parkinson’s disease presented with 3 months of progressive lower extremity edema and acute onset of altered mental status. On admission, he was somnolent and disoriented; examination showed symmetric lower extremity edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites without stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory tests revealed AST 3877 U/L, ALT 2939 U/L, total bilirubin 4.5 mg/dL, INR 3.8, white blood cell count 19.4×10^3/μL, platelets 63×10^3/μL, lactic acid 13.9 mmol/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, with a negative acetaminophen level and toxicology screen. Viral hepatitis panels, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and HIV testing were negative. A diagnostic paracentesis was negative for infection or malignancy. Tests for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, hemochromatosis, and Wilson’s disease were unremarkable. The patient developed hepatorenal syndrome requiring continuous venovenous hemofiltration.  
Lower-extremity Doppler ultrasonography demonstrated extensive bilateral femoral–popliteal and iliac vein thrombosis. IVC filter placement was aborted due to clot burden. Hepatic ultrasonography with Doppler showed hepatic vein thrombosis and reversal of portal venous flow. Contrast CT of the abdomen, thorax, and pelvis revealed thrombus extending into the right atrium. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large echodense mass in the right atrium with preserved left ventricular function. Cardiac MRI demonstrated a 10.6×5.0×5.6-cm heterogeneous pericardial mass invading the right atrium.

A 28-year-old man with a history of migraine disorder presented with several months of pain and swelling in the right mastoid area, with a recent subjective enlargement of the mass and increased pain. Noncontrast CT of the head demonstrated a 3.0 × 3.0 × 1.1 cm hyperostotic lesion of the outer table of the right calvarium without intracranial extension or adjacent soft-tissue mass. Because of the new-onset pain and subjective growth of the lesion, surgical excision was planned, and MRI with and without contrast was obtained. A small amount of fluid was noted in the right mastoid air cells, and mucosal thickening was present in the right ethmoid air cells. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and free T4, were within normal limits.

She had hypertension and a remote history of hemorrhoidectomy, dilation and curettage, colonoscopy, and gastroscopy; she was a heavy smoker. On examination, there was a 3 × 3 cm palpable mass in the upper quadrant of the left breast without overlying skin changes. No axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy was noted. Breast MRI revealed an ill-defined, deep retroareolar spiculated lesion measuring 3 × 1.5 cm with an early enhancement peak and associated architectural distortion; no axillary lymphadenopathy or skin thickening was identified (BIRADS IV). An excisional biopsy showed breast tissue containing cohesive nests of neoplastic epithelial cells within a dense lymphoid infiltrate. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that the epithelial cells were positive for cytokeratin AE1/E3 and negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2/neu; the background lymphocytes stained positive for CD3 and CD20.

A 48-year-old white man, a lifelong non-smoker with a remote bronchoscopic resection of a tracheal carcinoid 17 years earlier, presented with a three-month history of mild hemoptysis and cough without dyspnea. He also noted a non-tender, 2 × 2 cm subcutaneous mass on his left forearm without overlying skin changes. On examination, his vital signs were normal with an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, and coagulation profile, were all within normal limits. A chest CT scan showed a polypoid lesion in the precarinal tracheal region adjacent to the anterior wall. Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a mass arising from the anterior tracheal wall just above the main carina, causing an 80% obstruction of the right main bronchus and 70% obstruction of the left main bronchus. The lesion was resected bronchoscopically with electrocautery, restoring full airway patency without complication. On hematoxylin–eosin staining, the tumor consisted of large nests of eosinophilic cells within a collagenous and myxoid matrix, and a carcinoid tumor was initially suspected.

A 17-year-old boy presented on the fourth day of an acute febrile illness. He reported fever and severe myalgia for 4 days, productive cough with yellow sputum but no hemoptysis, and 3 days of watery diarrhea. On the day of transfer, he developed oliguria and noted red-colored urine. He denied trauma, exertion, medication ingestion, or freshwater exposures.

On examination, temperature 38.4 °C, pulse 102 bpm, blood pressure 100/80 mm Hg, GCS 15. He appeared unwell, with generalized muscle tenderness and restricted movement due to pain. Chest auscultation was clear bilaterally; the abdomen revealed right hypochondrial tenderness without hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic exam was normal.

Laboratory studies showed reduced ionized calcium 8.16 mg/dL, elevated phosphate 5.4 mg/dL, and normal magnesium. Initial abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. He was admitted to the ICU and treated with acetaminophen and empiric intravenous cefotaxime and clarithromycin. Over the next ten hours he developed sinus tachycardia up to 150–195 bpm and hypotension requiring fluid adjustments guided by central venous pressure and vasopressors. Chest radiograph and echocardiogram were unremarkable. A repeat abdominal ultrasound remained normal. Urinalysis showed no red cells, mild proteinuria, and 6–8 pus cells per high-power field. Serum creatine phosphokinase was markedly elevated at over 90,000 U/L.

A 66-year-old woman with a history of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma presented with abdominal and pelvic pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory studies, including a creatinine level of 0.81 mg dl–1, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right renal mass with areas of fat attenuation located in the upper pole, creating a defect in the renal parenchyma. The lesion contained visible vessels extending into the renal cortex, a finding known as a “renal parenchymal vascular pedicle.” Additionally, there was a fatty tumor thrombus within the right renal vein extending to its confluence with the inferior vena cava. No other masses or enlarged lymph nodes were identified.
